sourceBody:
Cover bare soil with suitable clean mulch, such as straw, dry grass or wood chips.

Mulch can reduce evaporation, soften the impact of rain and suppress weeds.

Keep it clear of trunks and stems. Check moisture underneath and adjust the layer; more mulch is not always better.

Cover crops can protect ground between main crops. Choose for local weather, available water and the next planting.

The course examples include oats, lupins, sunn hemp and cowpea. Check local suitability before sowing.

Legumes need suitable bacteria and growing conditions to fix nitrogen. Nutrients in their residues become available as the material decomposes.

Worm farms can turn suitable food scraps and bedding into castings. Check the bin rather than expecting a fixed harvest date.

Liquid that drains naturally from a worm bin is called leachate. It is not the same as a prepared worm-casting tea.

Leachate can contain harmful organisms or substances. Do not use it on edible plants or assume that dilution makes it safe.

A Highveld field left bare after the maize harvest faces two main risks.

Winter wind can carry away dry topsoil.

The first heavy spring storm can strike bare ground and damage its surface and structure. If water runs over the field, it can carry loosened soil away.

Cover crops, mulch, and organic matter can help hold soil in place and help it stay alive.

semanticChecks: The 13 exact canonical paragraphs match in order; the VE registry currently holds all 13 L3 body paragraphs in exact English, with no localized text to preserve.
Mulch wording retains suitable clean material and all examples; can remains explicit for each benefit, including softening rain impact and suppressing rather than eliminating weeds.
Trunks and stems remain distinct, mulch is kept from touching them without an invented spacing, and underneath moisture/layer adjustment/more-is-not-always-better remain.

Cover-crop protection remains between main crops; selection still depends on local weather, available water and the next planting. Course examples and order are oats, lupins, sunn hemp and cowpea; suitability is checked before sowing.

Legumes still need suitable bacteria and growing conditions to fix nitrogen; residue nutrients become available as material decomposes. Worm farms can process suitable food scraps and bedding into castings, with the bin checked instead of a fixed harvest date.

Natural drainage from a worm bin is distinguished from prepared worm-casting tea. Leachate can contain harmful organisms or substances; it is not to be used on edible plants, and dilution is not assumed to make it safe.

The bare Highveld field is specifically after maize harvest and faces two main risks. Winter wind can carry away dry topsoil. The first heavy spring storm can damage bare ground; water carries loosened soil only if it runs over the field.
Final cover crops, mulch and organic matter can help hold soil in place and help it stay alive; no benefit is guaranteed.
No species, crop, timing, amount, safety guarantee or new farming instruction was added.
